summary: A longest skewed path forces inspection through the final node to determine the maximum depth. The explicit depth-first traversal visits every node once and retains height-proportional pending state.

optimality.argument: Consider an n-node skewed tree. Without reaching the final node, an algorithm cannot distinguish depth n from a tree whose path ends earlier, so worst-case maximum-depth computation requires Omega(n) node visits. The current iterative traversal pushes and pops every node once with constant work per visit, giving O(n) time and O(h) auxiliary stack space.

replacement_checks.evidence: The last node of a skewed path determines whether the maximum depth is n or smaller, forcing a linear worst-case traversal.
Each node is pushed once, popped once, and processed with constant additional work; pending DFS state is bounded by height h.
The source-fidelity-verified examples cover branching and skewed trees; black-box real-test execution verifies every existing ordinary check without inspecting its definition.
